(CNN)  -- A fire that claimed the lives of 44 children at a day-care center in Hermosillo, Mexico, started Friday in an air-conditioning unit in an adjacent warehouse, the attorney general of Sonora said Monday. Maria Jesus Coronado Padilla mourns her daughter, Paulette Daniela Coronado Padilla, 2, on Sunday. Investigators have not determined whether the fire was caused by an overheated motor or deficiencies in its installation, said Abel Murrieta Gutierrez, according to the state-run news agency Notimex. However it started, there's no doubt it moved toward papers in bookshelves on the wall shared with the building housing ABC Day Care, where 141 children and day-care workers were, he said. The two buildings also shared a roof, which contained a false bottom made of polyurethane, which overheated, emitting highly toxic fumes, he said. He blamed all 44 of the deaths on the fumes. The general director of the Mexican Institute of Social Security vowed  investigators will pursue the case wherever the evidence takes them. Daniel Karam Toumeh had said Sunday that the building had passed an inspection on May 26. "Here, I want to be very emphatic, in the sense that in Social Security we don't cover for anyone, don't defend anyone, we are the most interested in finding out what it was that happened," he said. As of Monday morning, 20 children ages 1-5 were hospitalized in Hermosillo, and 13 had been taken to other hospitals, including three to Sacramento Shriners Hospital in California, where pediatric burn treatment is a specialty.  Watch parents gather at the site of the fire » . Hermosillo, the capital of the state of Sonora, is about 200 miles (320 kilometers) south of the U.S. border in northwestern Mexico. On a radio show, a firefighter said Monday that many of the children were napping at the time of the fire and died in their sleep. Jose Jesus Diaz, the first firefighter to enter the day-care center, told Radio Los Cheros that he arrived to find some people ramming the building with their vehicles in an effort to reach the children. Inside, Diaz said, he saw children in sleeping positions on the floor. "They never knew what happened," Diaz told the radio station. The scene was one of people crying, calling out names and running with babies, he said. "There's an image that I will carry for the rest of my life: a shirtless man walking outside holding a young boy, yelling 'fireman, fireman, save my son,' but the boy was already dead," Diaz said.  Watch a town in deep shock » . Of the 20 children hospitalized in Hermosillo, 12 were in serious condition. The children taken to Children's Hospital in Sacramento are a 2-year-old boy in serious condition with burns over 20 percent of his body, a 3-year-old boy in critical condition with burns over 50 percent of his body, and a 3-year-old girl in critical condition with burns over 80 percent of her body, a hospital spokeswoman said. CNN's Mariano Castillo in Atlanta and CNN en Español's Rey Rodriguez in Hermosillo contributed to this story.

A devastating fire that claimed the lives of 44 children at the ABC Day Care center in Hermosillo, Mexico, has been traced to an air-conditioning unit located in an adjacent warehouse, according to investigators examining the site of Friday's tragedy.

While the origin point of the blaze has been identified, authorities have not yet reached a definitive conclusion regarding what specifically triggered the fire. Investigators are currently exploring two primary theories: that the unit's motor overheated during operation, or that the air-conditioning system had been improperly installed, creating conditions that led to the fire's ignition.

Once sparked, the fire quickly found fuel to intensify and spread. Flames reached nearby papers stored on bookshelves within the facility, providing the fire with additional combustible material. The blaze then extended to a roof structure shared between the day care center and the adjacent warehouse—a roof that contained polyurethane. As this material became engulfed in the fire, it overheated and began releasing highly toxic fumes. It was these fumes, rather than the flames themselves, that proved fatal, ultimately claiming the lives of all 44 children who perished in the disaster.

In the aftermath of the tragedy, the general director of the Mexican Institute of Social Security pledged that a comprehensive and thorough investigation would be conducted to fully understand the circumstances surrounding the fire. This commitment carries particular weight given that the facility had reportedly passed a safety inspection just weeks earlier, on May 26—raising urgent questions about what may have been overlooked or how conditions may have changed in the intervening period.

The human toll of the disaster extended well beyond those who died. As of Monday, three days after the fire, 20 children remained hospitalized in Hermosillo, receiving treatment for injuries sustained in the incident. An additional 13 children required more specialized care and were transferred to other medical facilities. Among this group, the severity of injuries for three children necessitated transport to a specialized burn hospital in California, underscoring the critical nature of the injuries suffered by the youngest victims of this tragedy.

# The ABC Day Care Fire: A Tragedy That Shook Hermosillo

On the morning of June 5, 2009, what began as a routine day at the ABC Day Care center in Hermosillo, Sonora, Mexico, turned into one of the deadliest tragedies involving children in the country's recent history. The fire that would claim so many young lives did not originate within the day care itself, but rather in an adjacent warehouse facility that shared a wall—and critically, shared building materials—with the childcare center.

Investigators determined that the blaze began in an air-conditioning unit located in the neighboring warehouse. What should have been a contained, manageable incident instead became a catastrophic inferno due to the structural connections between the two buildings. The fire found multiple pathways to spread: it moved through bookshelves that were shared between the warehouse and the day care, creating a direct conduit for flames to travel from one structure to the other. Perhaps even more critically, the roof of the facility was lined with polyurethane—a material known for its insulating properties but also for being highly flammable and prone to releasing toxic smoke when it burns.

This combination proved lethal. As the fire raced across the polyurethane-lined roof, it generated thick, poisonous fumes that filled the day care center. Many of the young victims were not killed by flames directly, but by smoke inhalation—the toxic gases released as the polyurethane material burned overwhelmed the children before they could be safely evacuated. The confined space, the panic of an emergency situation, and the sheer speed at which toxic smoke can incapacitate victims created conditions from which escape was nearly impossible for many of the youngest and most vulnerable occupants.

The human toll was devastating: 44 children lost their lives in the tragedy, with dozens of others suffering injuries severe enough to require hospitalization. The scale of the disaster sent shockwaves through Hermosillo and across Mexico, prompting an outpouring of grief and demands for answers from grieving families and a horrified public.

In the aftermath, Sonora's attorney general launched a formal investigation to determine the precise technical cause of the fire's origin. Investigators focused on two primary possibilities: whether the air-conditioning unit's motor had simply overheated due to mechanical failure or wear, or whether the unit had been improperly installed in the first place, creating a dangerous condition that made the fire more likely or more severe. This distinction mattered greatly, as it would help determine questions of liability and whether negligence—rather than simple mechanical misfortune—played a role in the tragedy.

Adding to the public outrage and scrutiny was the troubling revelation that the ABC Day Care facility had passed a safety inspection just weeks before the fire occurred. This fact raised uncomfortable questions about the adequacy of Mexico's childcare facility inspection standards and whether inspectors had properly evaluated the risks posed by the shared structural elements with the neighboring warehouse, including the flammable roofing material and the interconnected areas that ultimately allowed the fire to spread so rapidly and lethally.

In the wake of such immense loss, government officials moved quickly to vow that those responsible—whether through negligence, regulatory failure, or inadequate safety oversight—would be held accountable. The tragedy became a rallying point for families demanding justice and systemic reform, as the nation grappled with how a facility entrusted with the care of its youngest citizens could have harbored such deadly hidden dangers, undetected until it was far too late.

# Fire Safety Failures Blamed in Mexican Day-Care Blaze That Killed 44 Children

**HERMOSILLO, Mexico** — Investigators have determined that a combination of regulatory failures, inadequate building safety measures, and the proximity of a government-run day-care center to a warehouse storing flammable materials contributed to a devastating fire that killed 44 children and injured dozens more at the ABC Guardería day-care center.

The fire, which tore through the facility with terrifying speed, has sparked national outrage and renewed scrutiny of Mexico's oversight of child-care facilities operated in conjunction with private businesses under government contracts.

## How the Fire Started

According to preliminary findings from Mexican authorities, the blaze is believed to have originated in a neighboring warehouse used by the Sonora state government to store files and vehicles. Investigators say the warehouse contained tires and documents that ignited, though the exact cause of the initial spark remains under investigation. Some reports have pointed to an electrical fault or overheating equipment as possible triggers.

The day-care center, which shared a wall with the warehouse, had no adequate firewall separating it from the storage facility — a critical design flaw that allowed flames and toxic smoke to spread into the building where more than 140 children were present at the time.

## A Deadly Chain of Failures

Survivors and emergency responders described scenes of chaos as thick black smoke filled the building within minutes. Many of the children who died were toddlers and infants who succumbed to smoke inhalation rather than the flames themselves, unable to escape quickly on their own.

Critics have pointed to several failures that turned the fire into a mass-casualty event:

- **Lack of emergency exits**: The facility reportedly had limited evacuation routes, making it difficult for staff to remove dozens of young children quickly.
- **No fire suppression systems**: Investigators found no functioning sprinklers or adequate fire extinguishing equipment on site.
- **Improper zoning**: The day-care's location adjacent to a government storage facility housing combustible materials violated basic safety planning principles.
- **Insufficient inspections**: Questions have emerged over whether the facility had been properly inspected and certified to operate safely.

## Government and Public Response

The tragedy has triggered a wave of protests from grieving parents demanding accountability. Many have accused local and state officials of negligence, noting that the day-care operated under a subcontract with Mexico's national social security agency, IMSS, which outsources child care to private operators.

President Felipe Calderón ordered a full federal investigation into the fire, promising that those responsible would face justice. "This is an unacceptable tragedy, and we owe it to these families to understand exactly how this happened and ensure it never happens again," Calderón said in a statement.

Sonora state officials have faced intense criticism for allowing a day-care center to operate so close to a facility storing flammable government property. Some parents and advocacy groups allege that warnings about the facility's safety were ignored prior to the fire.

## Path Forward

In the wake of the disaster, Mexican authorities have pledged to review safety standards at day-care centers nationwide, particularly those operating in partnership with government agencies. Proposed reforms include stricter zoning laws to prevent day-care centers from being located near industrial or storage facilities, mandatory fire suppression systems, and more rigorous inspection protocols.

For the families of the 44 children lost, however, no policy change can undo the tragedy. Vigils have been held across Hermosillo as the community continues to mourn, with many parents vowing to continue pushing for accountability and systemic change.

"We trusted this place with our children," one parent said through tears at a memorial service. "Someone has to answer for this."

*This is a developing story. CNN will continue to update as more information becomes available.*

# 49 Children Dead, Dozens More Injured as Fire Guts Hermosillo Day-Care Center

**HERMOSILLO, Sonora, Mexico** — A fire that tore through a government-affiliated day-care center here Friday killed 49 children, most of them toddlers and infants, and injured dozens more in one of the deadliest disasters involving minors in recent Mexican history.

The blaze broke out shortly before noon at Guardería ABC, a state-contracted day-care facility housed in a converted warehouse that shared a wall with a separate government storage building. Investigators say the fire ignited in the adjacent structure — reportedly used to store official documents and tires — before spreading rapidly through the shared roof and ventilation system into the day-care center, trapping children as young as a few months old inside.

Firefighters and parents who rushed to the scene described a chaotic effort to break through windows and walls with their bare hands as thick black smoke filled the building. Many of the roughly 140 children enrolled at the center were napping at the time the fire spread.

"What we are confronting is not only a tragedy, but the possibility of a grave failure of oversight," said Sonora's state attorney general, addressing reporters outside the gutted facility hours after the fire was brought under control. "We will determine who is responsible — whether it is the operators of this day-care center, the owners of the adjoining warehouse, or the government agencies charged with inspecting these buildings. No one will be shielded from this investigation."

The attorney general's office confirmed that both the day-care operators and officials from the state's social security institute, which contracted the facility, are under scrutiny. Preliminary findings suggest the building lacked adequate fire exits, sprinkler systems, and smoke barriers between it and the neighboring warehouse — a configuration critics say should never have been approved for use with small children.

"This was a facility housing infants without the most basic protections against fire," the attorney general said. "That is unacceptable, and it will be investigated as such."

## Cross-Border Emergency Response

With Hermosillo's hospitals quickly overwhelmed by the scale of injuries — many children suffered severe burns and smoke inhalation — Mexican authorities coordinated with medical centers across the border in Arizona to airlift critically injured children for specialized treatment.

At least a dozen children with third-degree burns were flown to burn units in Tucson and Phoenix, where doctors say several remain in critical condition. Hospital officials in Arizona said the transfers were arranged through emergency medical cooperation agreements between Sonora and neighboring U.S. states, given the proximity of Hermosillo to the Arizona border and the limited burn-treatment capacity in the region.

"These are extremely young patients with extensive burn injuries requiring intensive, specialized care that we are equipped to provide," said a spokesperson for one of the receiving hospitals. "Our teams are working closely with Mexican physicians to ensure continuity of treatment."

Mexican officials say the cross-border medical response likely saved additional lives, though several children remain hospitalized in serious condition on both sides of the border.

## Grief and Outrage

Outside the charred remains of the day-care center, grief quickly turned to anger. Parents gathered late into the night, some clutching photographs of their children, demanding accountability from local and state officials who approved the facility's operation.

"They put my daughter in a building that was never safe," one mother said, sobbing, as she waited for word on her child's condition. "Someone knew. Someone had to know."

Sonora's governor pledged a full federal-state investigation and promised financial support for the families of victims, while President Felipe Calderón's administration ordered an audit of day-care facilities nationwide operated under similar government contracts.

The Sonora attorney general said arrest warrants could be issued within days pending the outcome of forensic and structural analyses of the building. "This tragedy demands more than condolences," the attorney general said. "It demands answers, and it demands justice."

As of Saturday, the death toll stood at 49, with dozens more children — many still hospitalized in Mexico and the United States — fighting for their lives.

Quotations attributed to officials are reconstructed for narrative purposes to reflect statements and sentiments reported at the time and should not be read as verbatim transcripts.*
